vignette: Clinical Vignette for Daniel Daniel is a 46-year-old widowed auditor of Oceania descent who has been struggling with symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) following a devastating natural disaster. The event occurred six months ago when a powerful hurricane swept through his coastal town, destroying homes and claiming lives. During the storm, Daniel was trapped in his home as the wind howled outside, and he could smell the briny sea and taste the salty air as water seeped into every crevice of his house. Since then, Daniel has found that feeling happy or relaxed triggers vivid memories of the hurricane's fury. The night before a particularly busy day at work, he woke up in the middle of the dark with a racing heart, recalling the eerie silence just before the storm hit. This unusual silence had always made him feel something dangerous was about to happen, and now it haunts his nights. To cope, Daniel has turned to smoking cigarettes, finding that they provide a brief momentary escape from his intrusive thoughts. He avoids relaxing because he believes it makes him vulnerable to another disaster. Avoiding relaxation also means he's increasingly withdrawn from colleagues at work, preferring not to engage in casual conversation or even talk about the event with anyone. Daniel's fear of unfamiliar places has grown since the storm. When something takes longer than expected-like a traffic jam or a delayed train-he assumes the worst and feels an intense sense of dread. He believes he can't stop bad things from happening, which contributes to his feeling emotionally numb and disconnected from the world around him. The memory of the hurricane is so vivid that it feels unreal; sometimes when Daniel thinks about it, he smells the sea again and tastes the salty air. These sensory memories reinforce his belief that the world is a dangerous place, making him more anxious in unfamiliar situations. His heightened sense of threat also leads to frequent avoidance behaviors, such as skipping social gatherings or even avoiding certain parts of his neighborhood. Daniel's negative appraisals have become self-reinforcing over time. He feels helpless and emotionally numb, which makes it harder for him to engage with others or feel any sense of safety. His belief that the world is dangerous makes him more vigilant about potential threats, leading to increased avoidance behaviors. This cycle has caused significant strain on his work life; he's become increasingly isolated from colleagues and struggles to complete projects under tight deadlines. What finally brought Daniel to seek help was a particularly stressful day at work when he panicked after being delayed by traffic. He realized that these fears were affecting every aspect of his life, and the thought of continuing in this state became unbearable. The most significant fear for Daniel is losing control entirely; however, what he hopes for is a sense of safety and control over his life once again. Daniel's current state is marked by deep concern about his ability to function at work and in social settings. He has come to believe that the only way to regain some semblance of normalcy is through professional help, but his fear of feeling vulnerable holds him back from fully engaging with therapy. Despite this, he remains hopeful that with support, he can break free from the cycle of anxiety and threat monitoring that has taken over his life since the hurricane.
